name: Uma Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary day on the lines look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and still the junior hand on our electricity company's line crew. We meet at the depot at six, check the truck and insulating gear, then go where the work order sends us. I like seeing lights come back on, but climbing all day is harder on my knees than it was when I took the vocational course. I came into this trade late, so I'm still learning things the younger crew seem to know by touch.

say: I would welcome **quicker forms** if our crew still checks the pole and address.
I would tell colleagues that **line repairs** still need a person on site.
think: I worry that our **thin savings** leave us exposed even without a big AI change.
I trust my own **pole check** more than an app that once picked the wrong one.
do: Keep taking **regular shifts** and check each new work order against the pole sticker.
Skip **two café lunches** each week and use the money for the electricity bill.
feel: Relieved about **hands-on work**, but still worried about one injury wiping out our buffer.
S0.quote: The pole doesn't care how clever the form is; somebody still has to inspect it.
fieldNote: Uma's **relief** is tightly bounded by her current bills, rather than a broad belief that her job is secure.
She has already caught a **wrong pole number** in an app and uses that experience to justify checking every address.

steps.text: Keep taking line crew shifts and verify work orders against pole stickers
Skip two depot café lunches each week to pay the electricity bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the little AI forms are fine if they save us ten minutes at the depot. The pole doesn't care how clever the form is; somebody still has to inspect it. I wouldn't make a grand speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my problem is already the ordinary bills. My partner Dev works part time at a hardware counter, and between us we have less than a month's expenses put away. A quiet technology story doesn't fill that hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my shifts and put the work-order app through the same checks I use now. In the first year I'd ask the crew lead to show me any new form once, then use it if it doesn't muddle the address. I'd stop buying lunch at the depot café twice a week and put that money toward the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel a bit relieved that the job still needs hands. I'm not relaxed about money, though; one week off after a fall would empty our little buffer. The relief would be quite narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a form saved you time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the app filled in a pole number from a photo, but it chose the pole across the road. I caught it before we drove there, so I still read the sticker myself. A small shortcut is useful only when somebody checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev over supper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Dev we're staying with the shifts we have and skipping those two café lunches. Our grown children pay their own bills, which helps, but we can't ask them to be our emergency fund. Dev would understand the lunch money because we already count it.

say: I would urge the crew to learn the **planning screen** before new work orders arrive.
I would remind colleagues that **safe repairs** still require people at the line.
think: I expect **fewer shifts** could reach junior workers like me first.
I cannot pay for a **course fee** from less than one month of savings.
do: Practice the **planning screen** with Mara after a shift.
Enroll in **fault-finding training** if the company pays, and apply for depot inspection openings.
feel: Anxious about the **roster**, although I believe I can learn a new screen.
S1.quote: Learning a screen is doable; losing a shift is harder.
fieldNote: She names a believable **seniority risk** while keeping the line's physical safety work distinct from office planning.
The inspection application is a **knee-saving option**, but course enrollment depends on employer funding she does not assume.

steps.text: Practice the new work-order planning screen with crew lead Mara
Enroll in evening fault-finding training if the company pays the fee
Apply for depot inspection openings, including trial shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to learn the new work-order system before it lands on our tablets. If it plans routes and buys parts, the depot clerks will feel it before we do. The line still needs a safe crew, even if the paperwork gets faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'll squeeze the hours around the edges. I'm junior and slower at some repairs, so if the company sends fewer crews out, I won't be first on the list. I can't pretend our lower pay gives us room to sit out a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our lead Mara to let me practice the new planning screen with her after a shift. I use AI now and then to explain a manual, but I wouldn't let it decide if a wire is safe. In the first year, I'd take the evening fault-finding course at the training centre if the company pays the fee, and I'd apply for any depot inspection opening too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious, mostly about the roster. Learning a screen is doable; losing a shift is harder. I can take a small risk if I can still pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a depot inspection opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inspection still means looking at fittings and recording what you saw, and my knees could do with fewer climbs. There are only a few line jobs around here, so I can't just move to another utility. I'd apply even if I had to start with a trial shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for that course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the course fee would take most of what we have. My partner Dev's counter hours change each month, so I can't promise a payment plan. If the company won't cover it, I'd learn on Mara's screen and keep applying for inspection work.

say: I would ask who **signs off safety** when AI writes work orders.
I would tell the crew that **2031 robots** could threaten repair shifts after the office changes.
think: I expect **desk inspection** may vanish when thinking AI reaches full capability.
I fear losing my **line wage** before retirement, with almost no buffer.
do: Ask Mara for **fault-finding shifts** and apply to the water works maintenance team now.
Keep paid line shifts in **2029** while requesting a written redeployment route and cutting weekend travel.
feel: Alarmed by a **short bridge** between lost office work and robots reaching the line.
S2.quote: Three years is a short bridge when the other end may be gone.
fieldNote: Uma refuses to treat a **desk post** as shelter after full thinking AI, despite her interest in inspection work earlier.
Her **retirement date** gives little comfort because she says her savings cannot replace a wage at age 60.

steps.text: Apply now for water works maintenance positions
Keep taking available paid line shifts in 2029
Cut weekend trips to visit her grown daughter
Request a written company redeployment route before the 2031 robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company must tell us plainly which work orders the machine writes and who signs off on safety. By 2028 the office could be changed completely, while we're still up poles. By 2031, if the robots really handle the repair, our crew is exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. I'll be 60 when that thinking AI arrives, still junior, with no proper savings and maybe three years of climbing left before the robot can do it. I don't know if an inspection desk will even exist once AI can read the records better than I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask Mara for every safe fault-finding shift she can give me, and I'd put in applications for the maintenance team at the water works. In 2029, after the thinking AI arrives, I'd keep the paid line shifts I can get while asking the company for a written redeployment route before 2031. I'd cut the weekend trips to see our daughter, though I'd still call her every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one would keep me awake. Three years is a short bridge when the other end may be gone. I can picture Dev and me sitting at the table with the bills and no answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that redeployment request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what jobs remain after the office software arrives and whether lineworkers can be trained for them on paid time. I would want a date and a named person, not a poster in the canteen. Mara can pass the question up, but she can't promise a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you counting on retirement to carry you through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Retirement is in sight, but we haven't got a pot that replaces my wage at 60. My grown daughter has her own rent, and I won't write her into our budget. The water works application is a real try, not a guarantee.

say: I would say **five years** allows planning but guarantees no job.
I would ask the company and union to discuss **2031 and 2034** together.
think: I see **workshop repairs** as possible paid work while my knees allow it.
I cannot count on **stores records** surviving full thinking AI.
do: Get **retirement figures** from payroll and compare them with monthly bills.
Apply for **vehicle-check openings** and seek paid workshop training if offered.
feel: Worried, but less cornered because **five years** permits a real budget check.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to find out what our numbers really are.
fieldNote: She tests the longer timeline against **ages 63 and 66**, naming her knees as a constraint before robots arrive.
The proposed workshop path depends on **hands-on repairs** and paid training, while she expects its records to change.

steps.text: Apply for vehicle-check or tool-repair openings at the utility
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2032 while physically able
Take paid workshop training if the company offers a place
Trim grocery extras if the checked retirement figures fall short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years gives us a chance to make a proper plan, but not a promise of a job. In 2031 the software can take the checking and scheduling, and by 2034 the robots can tackle much of the field work. I'd want the union and company in the same room over the dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when the thinking work changes and 66 when the robots arrive. My knees might make climbing difficult before then anyway. I can imagine moving into stores or fleet work for a while, but buying and records could also be done by AI, so I'd look for the physical parts of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask payroll for my actual retirement figures and write our monthly bills next to them with Dev. I'd ask the maintenance supervisor about vehicle checks and tool repairs, and apply when a vacancy is real. In 2032 I'd take whatever paid line shifts remain, then seek paid training for the hands-on workshop role before 2034 if the company offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried but less cornered than in the two-year picture. Five years gives me time to find out what our numbers really are. It doesn't make the numbers better by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement figures are smaller than you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Dev and I would trim our grocery extras and keep working as long as my body lets me. I won't make the numbers look prettier by assuming a pension I haven't checked. I know we need a wage beyond 63 unless payroll surprises us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of workshop work appeals to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like repairing the crimpers and checking the truck before anyone takes it out. It's useful work I can put my hands on without standing up a pole in the rain. I'd still have to learn the workshop's tests properly.

say: I would tell younger workers to learn the **trade** while it still pays.
I would say **2036 AI** and 2039 robots require separate retirement plans.
think: I may still need **paid work** at 68, despite retirement being close today.
I fear needing a **ladder at 71** more than learning another form.
do: Get the **retirement statement** and transfer roughly twenty from each pay packet after rent clears.
Keep **tool-repair shifts** and review workshop applications with Dev in 2037.
feel: Less frightened, with a chance for **choices**, but uneasy about older-age physical work.
S4.quote: The thought of still needing a ladder at 71 makes my stomach turn.
fieldNote: A decade changes Uma's behavior toward **regular saving**, which she explicitly says she has not yet achieved.
She rejects an **office records refuge** and ties any 2037 workshop application to the household's measured need for wages.

steps.text: Transfer about twenty from each line pay packet after rent clears
Keep taking manageable paid line and tool-repair shifts
Apply for a part-time workshop opening in 2037 if wages are still needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to stop guessing about retirement. By 2036 the office's thinking work could be done by AI, and the line robots follow around 2039. I wouldn't tell the apprentices their trade is safe forever, but I'd tell them to learn it well while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 when full thinking AI arrives, I may have left the truck already, but I can't assume that. At 71 when the robots arrive, Dev and I may still need some income, and I don't know what either of us can physically manage. A decade helps only if we use it to put money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by getting payroll's retirement statement, then set an automatic small transfer from each line pay packet after the rent clears. I'd keep working and take the tool-repair shifts I can handle, rather than aim for an office records job. In 2037 I'd review our income with Dev and apply for a part-time workshop opening if we still need wages; by 2039 I'd stop climbing if a safe replacement is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the least frightening AGI version for me, though it's not peaceful. I would be proud if we reached that point with choices. The thought of still needing a ladder at 71 makes my stomach turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How small is that transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a fixed amount we can actually keep, perhaps twenty from each pay packet, and lower it if Dev's hours drop. I haven't managed a regular transfer yet. Starting with something honest is better than promising a large figure and borrowing it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them our plan, but I wouldn't ask for a monthly payment. Our son has a baby now and our daughter rents her own place. I want them to know if we're struggling, not carry the calculation for us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I'd have to find a new paid place before we'd built any savings, and even the inspection desk might disappear. A written company redeployment offer with paid training, plus a few months of wage support if shifts vanish, would give Dev and me breathing room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens if my knees give out before a robot ever arrives. I need the company to take that seriously now, not only when a machine can climb. A workshop vacancy with proper training would mean more to me than another clever tablet.

headlineQuote: A workshop vacancy with proper training would mean more to me than another clever tablet.
portrait: Uma is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** whose late entry into the trade makes roster cuts feel personal.
She and Dev have **under one month** of expenses saved, and their grown children have their own bills.
She checks **pole stickers** after an app once selected the wrong pole across the road.
She seeks **hands-on workshop work** as her knees age, while doubting records jobs will survive full thinking AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Uma too little time to replace her wage before robots reach line repairs.
whatWouldHelp: A written **redeployment offer**, paid workshop training, and temporary wage support would give her household room to adjust.
